Sheet 01 · Part 1

Key concepts

The one thing

Four lists and three definitions. That is the whole of Part 1.

The five integrated elements, the five characteristics of a project, the seven aspects of performance and the three delivery approaches — then what a project is, what project management is, and what project context is. Everything the method says later is said in these words.

The five integrated elements

PRINCE2 is built from five parts that only work together.

ElementWhat it is
PrinciplesThe seven guiding obligations that determine whether a project is genuinely being managed using PRINCE2. Unless all seven are applied, it is not a PRINCE2 project.
“Those working on the project and those affected by the project. An understanding of the needs, capabilities and motivations of the people involved and the relationships between them is crucial to how the project is established and managed.”
PracticesSeven aspects of project management that “must be applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle”. Each practice explains the specific treatment that aspect needs for the processes to be effective — and why it is necessary.
ProcessesSeven processes that “describe the entire project lifecycle, from activities before getting started, through the stages of project delivery, and to the final act of project closure. Each process has checklists of recommended activities and related responsibilities.”
The environment the project sits in. The principles, practices and processes “are applied by the people involved to ensure that the method is fit for the project context”.
Danger

Some practice questions in circulation still say there are four integrated elements.

There are five. Those questions are out of date — they reflect an older syllabus, which had four. When you meet one, count and back in.

What a project is

Official wording

A project is a created to deliver one or more business according to an agreed .

The five characteristics that distinguish a project from business as usual

CharacteristicOfficial wording
Change“Projects are the means by which we introduce change.”
Temporary“Projects are temporary in nature. When the desired change has been implemented, resumes (in its new form), and the need for the project is removed.” Because they are temporary “they should therefore have a defined start and a defined end”.
Cross-functional“Projects often work across the usual functional divisions within an organization and sometimes span different organizations.” A project “involves a team of people with different skills working together on a temporary basis to introduce a change that will impact others outside the team”.
Unique“Every project is unique. An organization may undertake many similar projects and establish a familiar, proven pattern of project activity, but each one will differ in a certain way” — a different team, customer, supplier, product, location or timeframe.
Uncertainty (riskier)“The characteristics already listed will introduce threats and opportunities over and above those typically encountered within . Projects are riskier than any operational aspects of an organization.”

Project management

Official wording

Project management is the planning, delegating, monitoring and controlling of all aspects of the project, and the motivation of those involved, to achieve the project objectives within the expected performance targets.

The seven aspects of project performance

These are the seven things a project is judged on. Every one of them can be given a , at project, stage and team level.

Learn this list verbatim

· · · · · ·

Official wording

Tolerances are set “against the seven aspects of performance (benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability, and risk) for the respective level (project, stage, team)”.

“Progress control involves measuring actual progress against the performance targets of benefits, time, cost, quality, scope, sustainability, and risk.”

Two traps, both commonly examined

Sustainability is the seventh aspect. It is a full tolerance area, documented in the and referencing the organisation’s environmental, social and governance () goals.

People is an integrated element, not an aspect of performance at all. This is a deliberate distractor.

The three delivery approaches

ApproachOfficial description
“Each of the delivery steps to create the products occurs in sequence, and the product is made available during or at the end of the project (for example, in a construction project where requirements gathering and design occur before construction starts).”
“Often, but not exclusively, used for product development where requirements gathering, design, development and/or coding, and testing occur iteratively throughout the lifecycle of the project. This approach is often referred to as an approach.”
“Some elements of the project use a linear-sequential approach, and other elements use an iterative-incremental approach.” For example: linear-sequential for building the infrastructure of a service, iterative-incremental for the customer portal users access it through.

PRINCE2 does not assume or require any particular delivery approach. Two knock-on effects surface in the plans practice:

  • On an project, “the project plan may provide multiple delivery stages in which the quality and are refined in parallel with development of the required products through the use of a ”.
  • On a project, “the should be sufficiently detailed to enable costs and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence”.
Trap

“” is not a delivery approach — it is a type of control, belonging to the progress practice. There are three delivery approaches and only three.

Why project management is used, and what PRINCE2 fixes

Organisations use project management because change delivered through normal line management tends to fail in predictable ways: unclear objectives and scope, no agreed justification, poor estimation, undefined roles, uncontrolled change, unmanaged risk, and stakeholders who were never engaged.

PRINCE2 exists to address exactly those failure modes — it forces a documented justification, defined roles across business, user and supplier, product definitions agreed before work starts, controlled with , and an explicit route for escalating problems.

Features and benefits of PRINCE2

  • Generic and flexible. Its “strength is its flexibility and the fact that it is not specific to a particular industry”, type of project, commercial model, project lifecycle, delivery method, product development, or engineering practice.
  • Widely recognised, with a common vocabulary. It “provides a common vocabulary for all participants, which encourages consistency and the ability to reuse project assets, facilitate staff mobility, and reduce the impact of personnel changes or handovers”.
  • It separates management work from specialist work. PRINCE2 tells you how to manage a project, not how to build the thing.
  • It is , , and — the four structural features that follow from the principles.
Trap

A common vocabulary is not a fixed vocabulary: “in general, it may be necessary to tailor the PRINCE2 Project Management terminology to what is common in the company or in the industry in which the project is taking place”, and it “may also involve adjusting the terminology to match terms used by the organizations involved”.

Project context

Projects do not run in a vacuum. A project may sit inside a (a set of related projects delivering a strategic change) or a (all the change an organisation is running). It may be internal, or delivered under a commercial contract between separate organisations — which changes who the “customer” and “supplier” are, and makes the commercial management approach matter more. It sits within a regulatory and legal environment, and within the culture of the organisations involved.

All of this is why tailoring is a principle rather than an optional extra.

Five lists to have cold

The five integrated elements · the five characteristics of a project · the seven aspects of performance · the three delivery approaches · the seven principles.

The method 1

PRINCE2definition

A rulebook for running a piece of work: who decides what, at which points, and on what evidence. It does not say how to build anything — only how to stay in control of the building.

In the proper languageA project management method built from five integrated elements: principles, people, practices, processes and project context.

Answer these out loud before you look anything up
  1. Name the five integrated elements. Which two are the ones you forget?
  2. Give the definition of a project word for word. Which two words does the whole thing turn on?
  3. List the seven aspects of performance, then name the three levels a tolerance can be set at.
  4. What is “people”, and what is “event-driven”? Neither is what it gets mistaken for — say what each one actually is, and where it belongs.
  5. Name the five characteristics of a project. For “unique” and “uncertainty”, say what the wording concedes that a careless reading would overstate.
  6. PRINCE2 gives everyone a common vocabulary. Say why that does not mean the words are the same on every project.
  7. Which four verbs plus one noun make up the definition of project management?
  8. Name the three delivery approaches, and say which one the method requires you to use.
Read this before the next sheet

Part 2 is the seven principles, and one of them — manage by exception — is built directly on the seven aspects of performance. Have that list cold before you go on, or the principle reads as a rule about paperwork rather than a rule about how much room you have.

Sheet 02 · Part 2

The seven principles

The one thing

Seven obligations, and one permission to adapt everything else.

The seven principles are the part of the method with no exceptions in it: apply all seven or it is not a PRINCE2 project. Tailoring is what lets the rest of the method flex, and the principles are what makes that safe — they say what must stay true however much you adapt.

What the principles are, and why they matter

The principles are guiding obligations. They are universal (they apply to every project), self-validating (they have been proven in practice) and empowering (they give practitioners confidence and the ability to influence). There are seven, and unless all of them are applied, it is not a PRINCE2 project.

Official wording

“To enable PRINCE2 Project Management to be used for such a wide range of projects, the method is flexible in how it can be used for any given project. Rather than prescribing what to do to align the method to the specific project, PRINCE2 Project Management offers guidance through principles.”

The principles are what makes tailoring safe: they say what must remain true however much of the rest you adapt. They are also “likely to be applied in different ways across projects within an organization” — same principles, different application.

“Cats Definitely Like Meals Made From Tuna”.

Learn from experience is numbered second and define roles third; the sentence takes them the other way round.

1 · Ensure continued business justification

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project has business justification sufficient to warrant investment to initiate the project and ongoing investment through to successful completion. If it does not, it should be stopped.”

There “must be a justifiable reason for starting a project, and the justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the lifecycle of the project”. The justification “drives decision-making to ensure that the project remains aligned with the sought and contributes to ”.

Cue words. Viable · worthwhile · still justified · value for money · stop the project · benefits still expected.

2 · Learn from experience

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project team actively seeks, records, and implements improvements as a result of relevant lessons learned from prior projects and throughout the life of the project. It applies them in future projects and shares them for others to apply.”

Three time horizons: lessons from prior projects, lessons during this project, and lessons passed to future projects — and shared with others. A is “information to facilitate the future of the project or other projects and actively promote learning from experience”.

Cue words. Lessons log · lessons report · previous projects · what worked last time · sharing knowledge.

3 · Define roles, responsibilities and relationships

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project has defined and agreed roles and responsibilities within an organization structure that engages the business, user, and supplier stakeholder interests.”

The three interests exist because “all projects have the following primary : the business, users, and suppliers. All three stakeholder interests need to be represented effectively in the project management team; this is reflected in the design of a .” Suppliers “may come from within the organization, or external suppliers may be used for their skills and knowledge”.

And the reason a project needs a structure of its own: “the day-to-day line management structures of the business may not be designed for, or suited to, project work.”

Cue words. Who does what · appointing someone · three interests · project board membership · an external supplier joining.

Danger

The name ends with relationships.

Material in circulation drops the word and calls this “defined roles and responsibilities”. That is not the full name, and relationships is not decoration — it recurs all through the element as “key relationships”.

4 · Manage by stages

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project is planned, monitored, and controlled on a stage-by-stage basis.”

A is “the section of a project that the is managing on behalf of the at any one time”. Managing by stages “ensures that the project is properly initiated before work starts on delivery of the project’s outputs”, and it “addresses the need to keep plans within reasonable ”.

Every PRINCE2 project has a minimum of two management stages: an initiation stage, plus at least one delivery stage.

Cue words. Stage boundary · next stage plan · decision point · reviewing before committing more money.

5 · Manage by exception

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project establishes limits of delegated authority by defining tolerances for performance against its plans.”

This works by “delegating authority from one management level to the next, by setting against the seven aspects of performance (benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability, and risk) for the respective level (project, stage, team)”.

Why it exists: it “provides for efficient use of senior management time as it reduces senior managers’ time burden without removing their control. This ensures that decisions are made at the right level in the organization.” PRINCE2 “enables appropriate by defining distinct responsibilities for directing, managing, and delivering the project and clearly defining accountability at each level”.

Trap

You escalate when a is forecast to be breached — not when something has merely gone wrong.

Cue words. Tolerance · delegated authority · escalate · exception · senior management not being bothered with detail.

6 · Focus on products

Official statement

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project focuses on the definition and delivery of products, in particular their user’s quality expectations and requirements.”

Agree what the are, and what “good” looks like for each, before deciding the activities to build them. The “describes the total output from the project as defined in the ”.

Cue words. Product description · quality criteria agreed up front · what we are delivering rather than what we are doing · scope creep prevented.

7 · Tailor to suit the project

Official statement

“PRINCE2 Project Management is applied and tailored to suit the project environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk.”

And the purpose of doing so: “to ensure that project controls are appropriate to the project’s scale, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and risk”.

Cue words. Proportionate · appropriate to this project · simplifying a process · adjusting terminology · a light-touch approach for a small project.

The classic confusion: manage by exception against tailor

Both talk about “appropriate controls”. Manage by exception sets tolerances and limits of authority; tailor makes the method itself proportionate to this project’s characteristics.

If the sentence mentions a threshold, a limit or escalation, it is manage by exception.

Tailoring: what can be tailored, and what cannot

You can tailor:

  • Processes — simplify them or elaborate them.
  • — combine them, change their format.
  • Roles — combine them, within limits.
  • Terminology.
  • The project controls themselves.

Two worked examples: “requiring only those quality activities that are appropriate to the delivery method and product characteristics”, and creating “a project management team that is appropriate to the needs of the project and the capability of the organizations and people involved”.

You cannot drop a principle. All seven must be applied or it is not a PRINCE2 project. The likewise “must be applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle” — what you adjust is the treatment they receive, not whether they happen at all.

Danger

An option reading “practices that are not relevant to the project can be excluded” is wrong.

That is wording from an older syllabus, and it does not hold here. Every practice is applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle; what changes is the treatment, not whether it happens.

The direction of travel: “tailoring supports the ability to adapt the PRINCE2 Project Management method to the people and organizations involved, rather than attempting to adapt them to the method.”

Tailoring: who is responsible

Official statement

“The project manager is responsible for tailoring and will make recommendations having consulted relevant lessons and standards.”

The proposes; the , as the body accountable for the project, agrees the approach as part of approving the .

Tailoring: where the decisions are documented

Official statement

“How PRINCE2 Project Management will be applied and tailored for the particular project is captured in the PID.”

Trap

Not the . Not the . Not the . All three are offered as wrong answers.

Factors that influence tailoring

Where it comes fromThe factors
From the principle statementProject environment · size · complexity · importance · delivery method · team capability · level of risk.
From the purpose of tailoringScale · complexity · importance · delivery method · team capability · risk.
Also“How the method is applied and tailored depends on the nature of the project and factors internal and external to the business” — regulation, standards, corporate policy.

Each of the seven sets out how it applies every principle. The organizing practice’s:

The method gets sized to the job in hand, so a small job gets a lighter version of it.

In the proper language

“PRINCE2 Project Management is applied and tailored to suit the project environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk.”

The purpose of doing so: “to ensure that project controls are appropriate to the project’s scale, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and risk”.

The trapManage by exception sets tolerances and limits of authority; tailor makes the method itself proportionate. If the sentence mentions a threshold, a limit or escalation, it is manage by exception.

0 of 7Principles, one at a time
The three stakeholder interests 1

The business, user and supplier interestsconcept

Whoever pays, whoever uses it and whoever builds it. All three have to have someone speaking for them.

In the proper language

“All projects have the following primary : the business, users, and suppliers. All three stakeholder interests need to be represented effectively in the project management team; this is reflected in the design of a .”

Suppliers “may come from within the organization, or external suppliers may be used for their skills and knowledge”.

What tailoring is 2

Tailoringconcept

Fitting the method to the job instead of bending the job to fit the method.

In the proper language

“To enable PRINCE2 Project Management to be used for such a wide range of projects, the method is flexible in how it can be used for any given project. Rather than prescribing what to do to align the method to the specific project, PRINCE2 Project Management offers guidance through principles.”

Tailoring “supports the ability to adapt the PRINCE2 Project Management method to the people and organizations involved, rather than attempting to adapt them to the method”. The principles themselves are “likely to be applied in different ways across projects within an organization”.

Factors that influence tailoringconcept

How much method you use is decided by what the job itself is like.

In the proper language

From the principle statement
Project environment · size · complexity · importance · delivery method · team capability · level of risk.
From the purpose of tailoring
Scale · complexity · importance · delivery method · team capability · risk.
Also
“How the method is applied and tailored depends on the nature of the project and factors internal and external to the business” — regulation, standards, corporate policy.
What can and cannot be tailored 7

The five things you can tailorconcept

What you are allowed to change when you fit the method to the job.

In the proper language

  • Processes
  • Management products
  • Roles
  • Terminology
  • Project controls

Two worked examples: “requiring only those quality activities that are appropriate to the delivery method and product characteristics”, and creating “a project management team that is appropriate to the needs of the project and the capability of the organizations and people involved”.

Tailoring the processesconcept

The steps can be made shorter, or fuller.

In the proper languageProcesses can be tailored by simplifying them or by elaborating them.

Tailoring the management productsdocument

The paperwork can be merged together, or written in a different shape.

In the proper language can be combined with one another, and their format changed.

Tailoring the rolesrole

One person can hold more than one job, up to a point.

In the proper languageRoles can be combined, within limits — creating “a project management team that is appropriate to the needs of the project and the capability of the organizations and people involved”.

Tailoring the terminologyconcept

The words can be swapped for the ones people here already use.

In the proper languageTerminology can be tailored — the method’s words replaced by “what is common in the company or in the industry in which the project is taking place”.

Tailoring the project controlsconcept

How closely the work is watched, and how often it has to report back.

In the proper languageThe project controls themselves can be tailored, “to ensure that project controls are appropriate to the project’s scale, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and risk”.

0 of 5Things, one at a time

What cannot be tailoredconcept

No rule can be dropped and no practice skipped. What changes is how much of each one you do.

In the proper language

All seven principles must be applied or it is not a PRINCE2 project. The likewise “must be applied consistently and throughout the project lifecycle” — what you adjust is the treatment they receive, not whether they happen at all.

DangerAn answer option reading “practices that are not relevant to the project can be excluded” is wrong. It is wording from an older syllabus and it does not hold here.

Who tailors, and where it is recorded 2

Who is responsible for tailoringrole

The person running the work proposes it; the people who authorise the work agree it.

In the proper language

“The is responsible for tailoring and will make recommendations having consulted relevant lessons and standards.”

The project manager proposes; the , as the body accountable for the project, agrees the approach as part of approving the .

Where tailoring decisions are documenteddocument

In the folder agreed before the real money is spent — the .

In the proper language

“How PRINCE2 Project Management will be applied and tailored for the particular project is captured in the .”

The trapThe , the and the are all three offered as wrong answers.

The principles inside the practices 1

The principles inside each practiceprinciple

Every practice shows how it applies all seven, one line each.

In the proper language

Each of the seven sets out how it applies every one of the seven principles.

  2. Name the three qualities claimed for the principles, and say what each one means.
  3. A question describes someone left alone inside agreed limits who goes back up only on a forecast breach. Name the principle — and name the one it is most often confused with, and the word that tells them apart.
  4. Give the official statement for tailor to suit the project word for word, then give the purpose of tailoring. They list almost the same factors: name the three words that differ.
  5. Three documents get offered as the place tailoring decisions are recorded. Name the right one, and name the three wrong ones.
  6. What is the minimum number of management stages on a PRINCE2 project, and what are they?
  7. Name the five things that can be tailored. Then say what can never be tailored away, and what changes instead.
  8. Which principle names three stakeholder interests? Name them, say who they are represented on, and say where a supplier can come from.
  9. The learn from experience statement covers three time horizons. Name all three, and say what the statement requires after them.

Sheet 03 · Part 3

People

The one thing

Definitions with neighbours, and the neighbours are the wrong answers.

Two ecosystems, inside against affected, change management against change control, collaboration against co-creation, leadership against management. Each pair is a real definition sitting next to a real definition, so knowing roughly what a word means is not enough here — the wording is the discriminator.

The two ecosystems

The human side of a project is framed as two overlapping ecosystems.

TermWhat it means
The wider organization or organizations the project sits inside — their existing structures, governance, policies, culture and ways of working.
The temporary community the project creates: the people working on it and the relationships between them.

The relationship between the two is stated directly: “projects unite people from organizations that already have defined organizational structures and corporate governance requirements. An understanding of the organizational ecosystem is required to successfully design the project organization and determine how the project ecosystem will develop as a distinct entity from the organizational ecosystem.”

Above both sits the — “the layer of outside the project team that sets the overall objectives and levels for the project and holds the accountable for meeting them”.

People within the project, and people affected by it

  • Within the project — everyone in the : , , , , , , , and the team members doing the work.
  • Affected by the project — “people within the business who are affected by the project, but do not work within the defined project team”. Their characteristic contribution is “integrating new products into their area of the organization”.
Trap

The is inside the project management team — they represent the user community, not the people merely affected by it. So are the project executive and the team manager.

If a question asks who contributes from outside the project team, none of the named PRINCE2 roles is the answer.

Change management — the people meaning

Purpose of the change management approach, in the PID

“To establish the target organizational state required for the project to meet its objectives together with the means by which the business will shift from the current state and through any interim states.”

Why it matters: “All projects result in a change from how people, organizations, and systems operate the current state to a future target state that incorporates the use of the project products. Effective is required to deliver this change.” A project can deliver a perfect product and realize no benefits at all if nobody adopts it.

When deciding how much detail to put in the change management approach, consider: the skills and capabilities required during and after the transition; which areas of the are likely to be impacted; the key relationships; the evolving ; and how best to transition.

The biggest terminology trap in the method

(people element, change management approach) = moving the organization to a target state so that benefits are realized.

(issues practice, issue management approach) = controlling modifications to the baselined products. There, “change” means “a modification to any of the approved products that constitute the ”.

Read the sentence and ask: is this about people adopting something, or about a document being altered?

Stakeholders and stakeholder engagement

Official wording

A stakeholder is “any individual, group, or organization that can affect or be affected by (or perceives itself to be affected by) the project”.

The perception clause is part of the definition and is routinely dropped from notes. Stakeholders sit inside or outside the business — “trade unions, customers, suppliers, communities, interest groups, banks, or the media”.

are “the people the needs to work closest with to ensure the success of the project”. They “may be the following: senior executives; those found in the user, supplier, or wider operational communities within the organization undertaking day-to-day tasks and decision making”. And “stakeholders at the interface with the project may change over time as the project evolves” — engagement is not a one-off exercise done in initiation.

in practice means identifying stakeholders, analysing their interests and influence, planning how to communicate with them, engaging, and measuring whether the engagement is working.

Culture

is “the set of shared attitudes, values, goals” of a group. It shapes how openly problems get raised, how people collaborate, and how readily change is accepted. A project inherits the culture of the organizations involved and, through the organizing practice, deliberately develops “the project behaviours and culture” of its own ecosystem.

Collaboration and co-creation

TermOfficial definition
“People from across the working together to achieve the project’s objectives.”
“A specific form of collaboration involving users and key influencers in the design of products and agreed ways of working to ensure they are adopted by the project and organizational ecosystems.”
Trap

Co-creation is not a synonym for collaboration — it is the narrower thing, with three qualifiers: who (users and key influencers), what (products and agreed ways of working), and why (adoption). Both appear as options in the same question.

Leadership and management

TermOfficial definition
“Motivating people to achieve a project’s objectives. On projects, this is best done through collaboration across the project ecosystem, persuading, influencing, and co-creating with a focus on managing key relationships and seeking regular feedback to ensure team members remain aligned to the project’s objectives and agree to joint ways of working.”
“Instructing the execution of tasks in line with agreed ways of working. Co-creating ways of working with project team members (and stakeholders) significantly improves people’s willingness to be managed in line with them.”
Trap

The adage “leaders do the right things, managers do things right” is not the official wording. The discriminating verbs are motivating (leadership) and instructing (management). Each is used as the distractor for the other, including in a NOT-style question.

Effective teams: diversity, capability and competence

Building “an effective team will require a diverse set of capabilities, competencies, and perspectives that match the requirements of the project”. Four points follow.

PointOfficial wording
Same capability does not mean same performance“Even when people technically have the same capabilities and competencies, they are likely to perform the same role differently. Sometimes, the same person may perform differently depending on who they are working with.”
Roles should be personalized, not standardized“Roles and responsibilities should reflect the capability, authority, and availability of the individual undertaking the work and should be considered through the lens of their key relationships. They should be reviewed in the event of any shifts in these key relationships and updated accordingly.” So generic, standard are unlikely to be effective.
Gaps are closed by upskilling, not by swapping people out“It is important to understand the competencies and capabilities of the people recruited or assigned to a project and ensure any gaps are identified and mitigations established to cover them, such as upskilling.” And: “ideally organizations would select the people needed to fulfil each of the required roles, but this is often not possible.”
Seniority can cut across the structure“It is not unusual for members of the project team to be more senior than the project manager, potentially causing hierarchical tension.”

Also: “some motivational factors may be outside of a project manager’s remit — for example, remuneration and career progression of project team members.”

Communication

Purpose of the communication management approach, in the PID

“To define and describe the means and frequency of communication with and receiving feedback from across the project ecosystem, supporting alignment and shaping of the project. It facilitates engagement with stakeholders through the establishment of a controlled and bidirectional flow of information.”

Three phrases carry it: means and frequency, receiving feedback, controlled and bidirectional. Communication here is explicitly two-way.

  • “Most communication within organizations occurs outside of formal channels. Therefore, it is best to accept this and provide information in multiple formats that people can share easily and provide multiple pathways for people to give feedback.”
  • “The communication management approach is likely to evolve as the project evolves and becomes more defined.”

How people integrate with everything else

Six of the seven principles have a people sentence attached to them, and every one of the six is a real quotation.

PrincipleThe people sentence
“There is valuable knowledge hidden within a project ecosystem. This requires a collaborative environment that encourages knowledge sharing throughout the lifetime of a project.” And: “people factors such as behaviours, culture, and relationships are difficult to document and are best learned through social learning.”
“Decisions should be made at the most local level where the knowledge needed to make and own those decisions resides. Decisions should be progressed through the levels when a decision has the potential to impact other areas of the project.” And: “the extent of delegation is often dependent on the level of confidence and trust that exists in the key relationships.”
Ensuring “people factors are continually addressed throughout the project’s lifecycle”.
“The stages of a project often mark a change in the influencers and any key relationships. They are good points to review how the project is planned to deliver.”
“Co-creating products, with agreed product descriptions, with the business, user, and supplier communities unites their different perspectives. This improves the development and adoption of the products into the business, reducing handover risks and ensuring that operational and maintenance issues are fully considered.”
“Tailoring supports the ability to adapt the method to the people and organizations involved, rather than attempting to adapt them to the method.”
The shortcut
  • Trust and confidence → manage by exception
  • Social learning and knowledge sharing → learn from experience
  • Co-creating product descriptions → focus on products
  • Changing influencers at boundaries → manage by stages
  • Adapting the method to people → tailor to suit the project

The two people management products

Management productPurpose
Establish the target organizational state required for the project to meet its objectives, and the means by which the business will shift from the current state through any interim states.
Define the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, the project ecosystem — a controlled, bidirectional flow of information.

Both live in the . Both are reviewed and adapted at stage boundaries, along with the and .

One is the world the work lands in; the other is the world the work brings into being.

In the proper language

  • Organizational ecosystem
  • Project ecosystem

An understanding of the organizational ecosystem is required to successfully design the project organization and determine how the project ecosystem will develop as a distinct entity from the organizational ecosystem.”

Organizational ecosystemconcept

Everything that was already there before the work started — how the place is set up and how it does things.

In the proper languageThe wider organization or organizations the project sits inside — their existing structures, , policies, and ways of working.

Change management 2

Change managementconcept

Getting people to actually take up the new thing. It has nothing to do with editing documents.

In the proper language

“All projects result in a change from how people, organizations, and systems operate the current state to a future target state that incorporates the use of the project products. Effective is required to deliver this change.”

The trapChange management moves the organization to a target state; change control governs modifications to baselined products. There, “change” means “a modification to any of the approved products that constitute the ”.

Change management approachdocument

The written plan for moving people onto the new way of working.

How much detail it needs depends on: the skills and capabilities required during and after the transition; which areas of the are likely to be impacted; the key relationships; the evolving ; and how best to transition.

Stakeholderconcept

Anyone the work touches, anyone who can touch the work, and anyone who merely believes they are affected.

In the proper language

A stakeholder is “any individual, group, or organization that can affect or be affected by (or perceives itself to be affected by) the project”.

They sit inside or outside the business — “trade unions, customers, suppliers, communities, interest groups, banks, or the media”.

The trapNotes routinely drop “or perceives itself to be affected by”. Without that clause the definition is wrong.

Key influencersrole

The few people you have to work closest with — and who they are changes as the work goes on.

And note: “stakeholders at the interface with the project may change over time as the project evolves and relationships develop”.

What an effective team requiresconcept

A mix of people whose skills actually match what this job needs.

In the proper language

Building “an effective team will require a diverse set of capabilities, competencies, and perspectives that match the requirements of the project”.

  • Same capability does not mean same performance

Same capability, different performanceconcept

Two people trained the same will not do the job the same way, and the same person varies with who they work with.

In the proper language“Even when people technically have the same capabilities and competencies, they are likely to perform the same role differently. Sometimes, the same person may perform differently depending on who they are working with.”

Sheet 04 · Part 4, section 4.0

Management products

The one thing

Learn where things live once, instead of seven times.

Every practice moves the same set of documents around, and a large share of what gets asked about a practice is really a question about which document holds what. Three families: an approach says how something will be run, a register or log says what happened, a report says how it is going.

How every practice is set out

All seven are treated the same way, and each is examined on the same six things.

  • Its purpose.
  • Its key relationships with the .
  • The that support it.
  • Its key concepts and definitions.
  • The guidance for managing it effectively.
  • Its technique.

The seven practices at a glance

PracticePurpose in a line
Business case Why?Judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable.
Organizing Who?Define and establish accountability and responsibilities.
Plans How, when, how much?Define the products and the means to deliver them.
Quality What good looks likeDocument the user’s requirements and establish how they will be met.
Risk What if?Identify, assess and control uncertainty.
Issues What now?Collect and assess issues, and control changes to the baseline.
Progress Where are we?Monitor against plan, forecast, and control deviations.

“Because Our Products Quite Rarely Interest People”.

What a management product is

“describe the information that will be required to manage the project”. They are not outputs — they “are created solely for the purpose of managing the project”.

Specialist products are what the project exists to deliver; management products are how you steer it.

The PID — project initiation documentation

Purpose

“The project initiation documentation gives the direction and scope of the project and (along with the stage plan) forms the ‘contract’ between the project manager and the project board.” It “provides the basis for [the project’s] ongoing management”; “it includes the project plan, the business case, and the frequency of highlight reporting”.

The is assembled during initiating a project and baselined when the project board approves it. It is reviewed and, if necessary, updated at every stage boundary. Changes to it are handled through the issue management approach.

What is inside the PID

Where it sits in the PIDWhat is there
The nine management approaches · · · · · · · · — each of them an approach.
PlusThe · the · the · the · the (including reporting frequencies) · the · the .
Rule of thumb

If the name ends in “approach”, it is in the PID.

And it describes how something will be managed on this project — its procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities.

The project log

Purpose

“To capture the continually changing records of issues, lessons, products, quality, risk, and other formal/informal actions or events.”

ComponentWhat it holds
The project manager’s informal record — actions, events, observations and minor issues not being managed formally.
Lessons identified, from prior projects and from this one. A is “information to facilitate the future of the project or other projects and actively promote learning from experience”.
“A record of identified risks related to the project, including their status and history. It is used to capture and maintain information on all the identified threats and opportunities relating to the project.”
“To log issues that are being managed formally, their current status, and date of closure.”
“To summarize all quality management activities that are planned or have occurred.” Used by the project manager and as part of reviewing progress.
“To list all products required of a plan and the status of those products.”

The project manager maintains the project log as part of controlling a stage.

The three-family test
  • “How will X be managed on this project?” — procedures, techniques, standards, responsibilities → a management approach, in the PID.
  • “What is the record / status / history of X?” → a register or log, in the project log.
  • “Telling someone how it is going” → a report.

The two nastiest pairs: quality register holds the inspections and their results, product register holds each product’s status; and the (the risks themselves) against the (the tailored procedure for handling them).

The project baseline

The project baseline is “the current approved versions of the management products and specialist products that are subject to change control”. A is “a modification to any of the approved products that constitute the project baseline”. Everything the issues practice does hangs off those two sentences.

Sheet 05 · Part 4, section 4.1

Business case

The one thing

Building the thing is the easy half. Proving it was worth building is this one.

A chain runs from what you build to what the organization wanted: output, change, capability, outcome, benefit, business objective. Every link has an official sentence, and the wrong answers are made by skipping one. Around that chain sit four documents, six moments in the life of one of them, and a four-step technique.

Purpose

Purpose

“To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable, and achievable as a means to support decision-making in its continued investment.”

Three adjectives, in that order.

This practice is the direct expression of the principle. Justification “is established at the beginning of the project through the creation of a business case and then kept under regular review and updated in response to the decisions and events that might impact the desirability, viability, or achievability of the project”.

Key concepts — the value chain

Official wording

“PRINCE2 Project Management projects deliver outputs in the form of products which are used to facilitate changes in an organization or for organizations. These changes create capabilities that lead to outcomes. The outcomes allow the organization(s) to realize the benefits that are explained in the business case for the project. Outcomes that are perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders may result in dis-benefits.”

Output → change → capability → outcome → benefit → business objective. A negative outcome gives a dis-benefit.

TermDefinition
Output“The tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity.” What the project builds.
Outcome“The result of change, normally affecting real-world behaviour and circumstances. Changes are implemented to achieve outcomes, which are achieved as a result of the activities undertaken to facilitate the change.”
Benefit“The measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that is perceived as an advantage by the investing organization and contributes towards one or more business objectives.”
Dis-benefitA measurable negative consequence: “outcomes that are perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders may result in dis-benefits”. Critically — “dis-benefits are expected consequences of an activity, whereas a risk is uncertain and may never materialize.”
Business objective“The measurable outcomes that demonstrate progress in relation to the strategy and to which the project should contribute.”
What an outcome leads to

An outcome leads directly to a — a measurable improvement defined in the business case — and the benefit is what contributes to a . It goes never from an outcome straight to a business objective.

Management products

ProductPurpose
“To provide a full and firm foundation for the initiation of the project.” Created in ; contains the outline business case.
“To document the business justification for undertaking a project, based on the estimated costs against the expected benefits to be gained and offset by any associated risks.”
In the PID“To define the benefits management actions and benefits reviews that will be established to ensure that the project’s outcomes are achieved and to confirm that the project’s benefits are realized.” Benefit reviews “should include assessing whether sustainability targets have been achieved”. Much of it runs after the project closes.
In the PIDHow the project’s environmental, social and economic objectives will be managed, measured and reported.

The business case lifecycle

The business case is not written once and filed. It runs from before the project exists to after it has closed.

WhenWhat happens to the business case
The is used to develop the outline business case, inside the project brief.
The outline is developed into the full business case and baselined as part of the .
During each stageThe keeps it under review — “the business case is kept under review” is an explicit objective of — and checks it when assessing progress, risks and issues.
At each Updated with actual costs, products delivered, benefits realized and the latest forecasts, so the can confirm continued justification before approving the next stage.
Checked to “assess the project’s performance against requirements and the probability that the outcomes will provide the expected benefits”. Remaining benefit reviews are handed to the business, in the benefits management approach.
After closureReviewed by the business in a post-project benefits review, to confirm whether the intended benefits were realized in practice.

Aligning products to business objectives and tolerances

“Ultimately, the outcomes and benefits to be achieved from the project need to align with and contribute to the business objectives. These may include environmental, social and governance () goals set by the organization. The sustainability performance targets and tolerances for the project, documented in the business case, should reference and contribute to the ESG goals of the organization.”

is “the permissible deviation in the benefit performance targets that is allowed before the deviation needs to be escalated to the next level of management. Benefits tolerance is documented in the business case.”

“For benefits to be realized, the outcomes must be achieved, which means that the outputs from the project are used as intended, new capability is defined, and barriers to the use of the new capability are identified. A problem that commonly occurs is that projects are often successful from a delivery perspective but fail from an investment perspective.”

Establishing business justification

Official wording

“The business case should include not only the costs of developing the project product but also any changes to operational costs when the project concludes.”

“All seven aspects of the project’s performance targets and their relationships with each other should be considered as part of assessing the business justification, but there will often be trade-offs between different performance aspects. For example, if in developing the project product description it is decided that higher quality targets are required, it is likely to impact the cost, time, or sustainability targets.”

The seven are the , and raising one target usually moves another.

The technique: business case management

Four steps. The names matter.

StepWhat happens
1 DevelopStarting up a project“The provision of a project mandate activates the process of starting up a project. The project mandate is then used as an input to develop the initial business justification for the project documented in the outline business case.”
2 CheckProject manager, throughout — including at closure“The business case may undergo further refinement and will be updated across stages as project costs, timescale, products, and risks are further understood.” The project manager checks it “when assessing progress, risks, and issues to determine their impact on the business justification” and “during the final stage, as part of ‘closing a project’, to assess the project’s performance against requirements and the probability that the outcomes will provide the expected benefits”.
3 MaintainProject manager, at stage boundaries“The project manager updates the business case with the progress data (such as products delivered, project costs, benefits realized) and the latest forecasted benefits and performance targets.”
4 ConfirmThe business, after the project has closed“The business will review the business case as part of a post-project benefits review to determine the project outcomes in realizing their benefits. They will also assess whether the intended benefits have been realized in practice.”

The four in order, and the letters spell nothing — DCMC.

The second step is not “verify”

A great deal of the material in circulation gives step 2 as verify. It is check. Verify is wording from an earlier version of the method and it survives all through older notes.

Check against confirm

Check covers closure, and the project manager does it; confirm happens after the project no longer exists, and it is done by the business. Reviewing performance during is the check step.

The practice 2

Business case (the practice)practice

The part of the work that keeps asking whether this is still worth doing, and does not stop asking once it has started.

In the proper language

“To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable, and achievable as a means to support decision-making in its continued investment.”

Desirable, viable and achievable — three adjectives, in that order.

The business case practice and the principlespractice

This is where one of the seven rules actually gets done: write the argument down, then keep checking it.

In the proper languageThe direct expression of the principle. Justification “is established at the beginning of the project through the creation of a business case and then kept under regular review and updated in response to the decisions and events that might impact the desirability, viability, or achievability of the project”.

The value chain 6

The value chainconcept

What you build only counts once it is used, and something measurable improves because of it.

In the proper language

“PRINCE2 Project Management projects deliver outputs in the form of products which are used to facilitate changes in an organization or for organizations. These changes create capabilities that lead to outcomes. The outcomes allow the organization(s) to realize the benefits that are explained in the business case for the project. Outcomes that are perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders may result in dis-benefits.”

Output → change → capability → outcome → benefit → business objective. A negative outcome gives a dis-benefit.

The trapAn outcome leads to a benefit, and the benefit is what contributes to a business objective — never from an outcome straight to a business objective.

Outputdefinition

The thing that got built and handed over. On its own it proves nothing.

In the proper language“The tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity.” What the project builds.

Outcomedefinition

What people now do differently because of it. If nobody changed how they work, there is no outcome.

In the proper language“The result of change, normally affecting real-world behaviour and circumstances. Changes are implemented to achieve outcomes, which are achieved as a result of the activities undertaken to facilitate the change.”

Benefitdefinition

The measurable improvement that follows the change — not “we launched it” but a number that moved.

In the proper language“The measurable improvement resulting from an outcome that is perceived as an advantage by the investing organization and contributes towards one or more business objectives.”

Dis-benefitdefinition

A measurable downside you already know is coming, and have decided the rest is worth it anyway.

In the proper languageA measurable negative consequence of an outcome: “outcomes that are perceived as negative by one or more stakeholders may result in dis-benefits”.

The trapDis-benefits are expected consequences of an activity, whereas a risk is uncertain and may never materialize.

Business objectivedefinition

What the organisation is trying to get better at overall. The benefits are meant to add up to these.

In the proper language“The measurable outcomes that demonstrate progress in relation to the organization’s strategy and to which the project should contribute.”

Delivered against worth itconcept

Delivered on time and still not worth it is a real outcome, and a common one.

In the proper language

Establishing business justification 2

Counting what it costs to build is not enough. What it costs to run afterwards counts too.

Pushing one target up pushes another one out. They are weighed together, not one at a time.

For example, if in developing the project product description it is decided that higher quality targets are required, it is likely to impact the cost, time, or sustainability targets.”

Sheet 06 · Part 4, section 4.2

Organizing

The one thing

Five lists, and every wrong answer is another member of the same list.

Three interests, four management levels, eight roles, three documents, five technique steps. Almost nothing here is hard on its own — the whole difficulty is that the neighbours are all real, so knowing roughly who does what is not enough. The two that carry the most weight: who is accountable against who is responsible, and how much room each level has before it must ask.

Purpose

Purpose

“To define and establish the project’s structure of accountability and responsibilities (the ‘who’).”

Two names for one practice: the purpose sentence says the organization practice, the practice itself is called organizing.

The three project interests

“All projects have the following primary stakeholders: the business, users, and suppliers. All three stakeholder interests need to be represented effectively in the project management team; this is reflected in the design of a .”

InterestWhat it cares about
BusinessProject executive“Projects are created to meet a business need, which needs to be continuously justified as value for money throughout the lifetime of the project.”
UserSenior userThose who will use the products, operate them, or realize the benefits from them.
SupplierSenior supplierThose providing the skills and resources to build the products. They “may come from within the organization, or external suppliers may be used for their skills and knowledge”.

The four management levels

“The project is between four management levels against tolerances for seven .”

LevelResponsible for
CommissioningThe business layer, outside the project team“Defining the project level tolerances”; setting the overall requirements; holding the accountable.
DirectingProject boardOverall direction within the constraints set by the ; “determining whether to authorize any deviation that breaches or is forecast to breach the agreed stage tolerances”.
ManagingProject manager“Day-to-day control of a stage within the tolerance limits established by the project board.”
DeliveringTeam manager“Control for a , but only within the work package tolerances agreed with the project manager.”

The PRINCE2 roles

RoleKey facts
“Accountable to the business for the success of the project and has the authority to direct the project within the remit set by the business.” The business, user and supplier interests are brought together on it. It is the ultimate authority for approving changes.
“Appointed by the business as the single point of accountability for the project and is ultimately accountable for the success of the project.” Secures the funding. Owns the . There is only one, and they are appointed first.
“Accountable for ensuring that user needs are specified correctly and that the solution meets those needs.” Also responsible for “the successful handover and adoption of products into the business and continued realization of benefits after the project has closed”, and for securing ongoing commitment from the user community.
“Accountable for the quality of the products delivered by the suppliers and for the technical integrity of the project.”
“Has the authority to run the project on behalf of the project board within the agreed stage tolerances and constraints.” Responsible for , and for making recommendations “having consulted relevant lessons and standards”.
Delivers “the products to the agreed specifications”. “Coordinates an area of work that will deliver one or more of the that form the .” May be internal or external. Optional — the project manager can do it.
“Project board members are accountable for their respective areas of concern (business assurance, user assurance, supplier assurance). The project board is responsible for establishing how project assurance will be undertaken, ensuring clarity in the roles and responsibilities and how those appointed to assurance roles will interact with each other.”
“Responsible for providing services, such as administrative support, facilitating meetings and workshops, advice and guidance on the project tools, planning support, risk management, issue management, and change management.”

Project team against project management team

The project team is all people allocating time to it; the management team is board, manager, assurance, support.

The is “all people required to allocate their time to the project”. The is “composed of the project board, project manager, team managers, and project assurance and project support roles”. It cannot direct the project; the board does.

Work breakdown structure

A is “a hierarchy of all work to be done during a project that forms a link between the and the … supporting the project manager in determining how to structure project teams and the boundaries between them”.

Which practice the WBS belongs to

It is an organizing concept, not a plans one, and its purpose is about structuring teams. It has nothing to do with the realizing benefits after the project.

Management products

ProductPurpose
In the PID“To define who is involved and their relationships, and how they will work together.”
In the PIDDescribe “the roles of those in the project management team and their specific responsibilities”. These “should include specific accountability for targets”.
In the PIDHow commercial and supplier relationships are managed — contracts, procurement, and moving capability on and off the project.

The technique: organizational design and development

Five steps.

StepWhat happens
1 Understand the organizational ecosystem“Projects unite people from organizations that already have defined organizational structures and corporate governance requirements. An understanding of the is required to successfully design the project organization.” Clarify who retains responsibility for policies and procedures and ways of working.
2 Design the project ecosystem“Project organizational design describes how to organize work and people to achieve the project’s objectives. This includes: determining the effective structure of the team; determining the people and resources needed; implementing integrated working practices; developing the project behaviours and .”
3 Develop the project ecosystem“Implementing the design, and adapting and evolving it as the project progresses… ensuring the project is set up to deliver its objectives and to continuously improve. The development activities may include: onboarding people to the project, for example, a site visit, induction, or certification.”
4 Manage the ongoing changes to the project ecosystem“The capabilities required on a project will change over the project lifecycle, requiring the project manager to ensure the supports this, transitioning people onto and off the project as required, and enhancing capacity and capabilities.”
5 Transition the project into the organizational ecosystemAt close, understand the ecosystem the products and remaining team members will transition into. “There are three key aspects the project board needs to consider as part of the transition: products, people, and learning.”

The part of the work that settles who answers for what, and to whom, before anyone starts.

In the proper language“To define and establish the project’s structure of accountability and responsibilities (the ‘who’).”

Sheet 07 · Part 4, section 4.3

Plans

The one thing

Four tables, and the traps are all about what a thing is not.

Three levels of plan and a fourth thing that is not a level; four key concepts, two of which are wider than they look; three management products; four technique steps that swallowed an older technique whole. Almost every mark on this sheet turns on a boundary — scope includes managing, dependencies are between products, the exception plan is a type and not a level, and product-based planning is a step and not a technique.

Purpose

Purpose

“To facilitate communication and control by defining the products to be delivered (the ‘what’) and the means to deliver them (the ‘who’, the ‘how’, the ‘where’, and estimates of the ‘when’ and for ‘how much’) to satisfy the project business case (the ‘why’).”

Levels and types of plan

There are three levels of plan. The is a type of plan, not a fourth level — it is produced to replace one of them.

PlanWhat it is
Project manager, owned by the project board“A high-level plan showing the major products of the project and when, how, and at what cost they will be delivered.” Created during and baselined on approval by the . It “provides a against which to monitor progress throughout the life of the project”.
Project manager“A detailed plan used as the basis for project management control throughout a stage”, “based on more precise estimates that are achievable within the ”. Prepared near the end of the previous stage.
Team manager“A plan used as the basis for organizing and controlling the work of a team when executing a .” Optional.
Project manager, on the board’s requestProduced when a plan is forecast to breach its tolerance, to replace it. Written to the same level of detail as the plan it replaces, and created based on how the decides to address the exception.
Purpose of a plan, any type

“To provide a proposal that outlines the what, where, when, how, and by whom the project as a whole (or a subset of its activities) will be performed.”

This covers project, stage, team and exception plans alike.

Key concepts

TermDefinition
“The sum of product, delivery, and management activities represented by an approved plan and its and .”
“The sequencing, interrelationships, and duration of work packages and their associated tasks are captured in a schedule. All work packages for a stage must be included in the schedule for the stage.”
“A dependency means that one product is dependent on another. There are at least two types of dependency relevant to a project: internal and external.”
You can only plan in detail as far ahead as you can reliably foresee. Hence a high-level project plan plus a detailed stage plan for the current stage. “The PRINCE2 Project Management principle of addresses the need to keep plans within reasonable planning horizons.”
Trap

Dependencies are between products, not activities — and the count is “at least two types”, not exactly two.

Scope is broader than “products plus the work”: it includes management activities, and it is defined by the plan’s product descriptions and work package descriptions.

Management products

ProductPurpose
“To describe the project’s major products and intended purpose, including the user’s quality expectations and the acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project. It is created in the process of ‘’ and refined during the process of ‘’.”
“To describe how one or more products will be produced and delivered. It is used to pass responsibility for work formally to a or team member.”
See above — project, stage, team or exception.

Guidance: project stages

Minimum two stages. “For a simple project with a small number of well-understood products and mature delivery method, only two stages may be required. These are an initiation stage to prepare the project initiation documentation and a single delivery stage.”

Iterative-incremental projects often need more. “For an iterative-incremental project, the project plan may provide multiple delivery stages in which the quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development of the required products through the use of a product backlog.”

“leads to a plan based on the creation and delivery of the required products”. It “assists with clearly and consistently identifying and documenting the products to be produced by the plan and the interdependencies between them” and “reduces the risk of scope being neglected or overlooked”.

It does not address the planning horizon — that is .

Tolerances are set on all seven , “for the respective level (project, stage, team)”, to manage the project’s constraints.

Delivery targets are planned in, not bolted on: product descriptions carry sustainability requirements as acceptance criteria or quality specifications.

The technique: the PRINCE2 planning technique

StepWhat happens
1 · Defining and analysing productsWrite the — “in the process of starting up a project, the major products or outcomes, along with key quality requirements, are documented in the project product description”. Then break the project product down and write the individual . On a project “the product descriptions should be sufficiently detailed to enable costs and time to be estimated at an appropriate level of confidence”.
2 · Organizing work packages“When the delivery method is decided, the delivery activities involved in each product can be identified and organized into work packages.” Dependencies between products are identified here.
3 · Preparing estimates“Project managers and team managers always plan using estimates” — of people, and of resources. People: “the specific skills required, the level of effort involved, and when and where they will be needed”. Resources: “specific materials, equipment, facilities, access, natural resources, or money, as well as the number or amount of each”.
4 · Preparing a schedule“The sequencing, interrelationships, and duration of work packages and their associated tasks are captured in a schedule. All work packages for a stage must be included in the schedule for the stage.”

Material in circulation is wrong

A great deal of the material in circulation presents product-based planning as its own four-step technique — project product description, product breakdown structure, product descriptions, product flow diagram. It is not a technique of its own. Those activities sit inside step 1, defining and analysing products.

The project product description is written in defining and analysing products. Estimates of people and equipment are made in preparing estimates.

Sheet 08 · Part 4, section 4.4

Quality

The one thing

Six concepts, five places they live, and one question underneath all of it: which document holds this?

The location test is the sheet. Expectations and acceptance criteria belong to the whole project and sit in the project product description; specifications and tolerances belong to one product and sit in its own product description; the approach holds the method, the quality register holds what was checked, the product register holds what exists. Then one contrast worth a mark on its own: quality assurance checks the process from outside, project assurance is the board’s own.

Purpose

Purpose

“To document the user’s requirements of the project products and to establish the means by which they will be met.”

Two halves: write down what is wanted, and set up how it will be delivered and checked.

The practice “addresses the quality concepts, guidance, techniques, management products, and responsibilities for the project products”, and “quality is concerned with ensuring that the project products meet the user’s requirements and expectations and enable the desired benefits to be realized”.

Material in circulation is wrong

A great deal of the material in circulation gives the purpose as “to ensure products are fit for purpose”. True in spirit, and not the wording. The purpose is to document the user’s requirements of the project products and to establish the means by which they will be met, and that is the sentence that is quoted.

Key concepts

TermDefinition
“A need or expectation that is documented in an approved management product.”
Project product description“A statement about the quality expected from the project product, captured in the .”
Project product description“A prioritized list of criteria that the project product must meet before the user will accept it” — measurable definitions of the attributes required for the products to be acceptable to key stakeholders.
Each product description“A description of the quality measures that will be applied by those performing quality control and the levels that a finished product must meet.” They are stated in .
Product description“The permissible deviation in a product’s quality that is allowed before the deviation needs to be escalated to the next level of management.”
“The person or group responsible for assessing if a product meets its quality or acceptance criteria.”
The location test
The user’s quality expectations and the acceptance criteria — the whole project.
That product’s quality specifications, tolerances, method and responsibilities.
The techniques, standards and responsibilities used across the project.
The planned and completed quality activities and their results.
Every product required by a plan, and its status.

Management products

ProductPurpose
“Describe a product’s purpose, composition, where it is derived from, and quality specifications. It is produced during planning as soon as possible after the need for the product is identified.”
PID“To describe the quality techniques and standards to be applied and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality specifications and acceptance criteria during a project.”
Project log“To summarize all quality management activities that are planned or have occurred. The quality register is used by the and as part of reviewing progress.”
Project log“To list all products required of a plan and the status of those products.”

Guidance: planning, control and assurance

Quality planning. The “should identify all the major products to be delivered” — “this coverage is crucial to avoid the introduction of requirements outside the approved scope of the project in developing product descriptions”.

belongs here. “Product descriptions should include product sustainability requirements captured as acceptance criteria or quality specifications. Product sustainability considers both the environmental impact of the product and the characteristics that will ensure that the product can sustain the realization of its benefits over its expected lifetime.”

Expect requirements to change. “No matter how thoroughly and accurately stakeholder requirements have been captured in product descriptions in the process of , the project management team should anticipate requirements changes and be prepared to handle them.”

Changes to the baselined arising from lower-level planning “should be addressed using the ” — not through the quality route.

A product-based approach to requirements “helps avoid expending resources on work that cannot be traced back to the project’s business justification”.

Quality control is “the procedures to monitor the specific products of a project and their development or delivery activities to determine whether they comply with relevant standards and of identifying ways to minimize causes of unsatisfactory performance”.

“The provides a record of quality control activities, starting with the approval of each product description. As the project progresses and records of the quality control activities are completed, the quality register is updated to reflect (in summary form) the actual results from the quality activities.”

Quality assurance is an independent check that the project is being run properly — a check on the process, usually performed from outside the project team, for example by a corporate or programme function.

Trap

Quality assurance checks the process, from outside; project assurance is the project board’s own.

“Project board members are accountable for the assurance of their respective areas of concern (business assurance, user assurance, supplier assurance).”

Three-way shortcut

Planning sets the criteria · control checks the products · assurance checks the process, independently.

The technique: quality management

Structured as quality planning — which itself contains several numbered activities, including the two named below — then controlling quality, then accepting products.

StepWhat happens

The quality register merely records the quality control activity and its result (typically as ‘pass’ or ‘fail’). Accepting products“Acceptance of a project product typically transfers ownership or responsibility for the product from the project or supplier to the on behalf of the user.” Reviewing the project product against the user’s quality expectations and acceptance criteria happens here.

Within controlling quality, the person doing the checking is the — “the person or group responsible for assessing if a product meets its quality or acceptance criteria”.

The review against acceptance criteria is not in planning — it is in accepting products.

The practice 1

Quality (the practice)practice

The part of the work that settles what would count as done properly, and how that gets checked.

In the proper language

“To document the user’s requirements of the project products and to establish the means by which they will be met.”

It “addresses the quality concepts, guidance, techniques, management products, and responsibilities for the project products”, and “quality is concerned with ensuring that the project products meet the user’s requirements and expectations and enable the desired to be realized”.

DangerA great deal of the material in circulation gives the purpose as “to ensure products are fit for purpose”. True in spirit, and not the wording. The purpose is to document the user’s requirements of the project products and to establish the means by which they will be met.

Whoever decides whether it passed.

In the proper language“The person or group responsible for assessing if a product meets its quality or acceptance criteria.” Within controlling quality, the reviewer is the person doing the checking.
