Sheet 09 · Part 4, section 4.5

Risk

The one thing

The longest sheet in the pack, and almost all of it is pairs that are nearly the same.

Eleven key concepts, four biases, ten responses, five procedure steps. The marks are in the near-misses: appetite is an attitude and tolerance is a measurable threshold; the risk owner holds the whole risk and the action owner holds one action; the approach holds the procedure and the register holds the risks. And two facts about the response table on their own: transfer has no opportunity twin, and the twin of accept is reject.

Purpose

Purpose

“To identify, assess, and control uncertainties that would affect the project’s objectives, and, as a result, improve the ability of the project to succeed.”

Improve the ability to succeed. “There is no guarantee that the agreed objectives would be met.”

Trap

Uncertainty runs both ways: a threat has a negative impact, an opportunity has a positive one. Risk is not only about avoiding bad things.

Key concepts

TermDefinition
“An uncertain event or set of events that, should they occur, will affect the achievement of objectives.” Measured by “a combination of the probability of a perceived threat or opportunity occurring and the magnitude of its impact on objectives”.
“Opportunity” is used “for uncertain events that would have a positive impact on objectives”; a threat is the negative counterpart.
A well-written risk names all three: the situation, the uncertain thing, the impact — the cause that gives rise to it, the event that may happen, and the effect on objectives if it does.
The organization’s attitude towards risk-taking — how much risk it is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
“A measurable threshold to represent the tolerable range of outcomes for each objective ‘at risk’, using the same units as for measuring performance for that objective.”
“The degree to which a particular objective is at risk.”
“The probability that the risk will occur (often estimated by considering its likelihood or frequency).”
“The estimated effect on objectives should a risk occur.”
“The person who is responsible for the management, monitoring, and control of all aspects of a particular risk assigned to them, including the implementation of the selected responses to address the threats or to maximize the opportunities.”
“The nominated owner of agreed actions to respond to a risk. This role is also known as the risk actionee.” May be the same person as the risk owner, or not.
“A sum of money to fund specific management responses to the project’s threats and opportunities (for example, to cover the costs of any contingent plans should a risk materialize).”
Trap

Appetite against tolerance. Appetite is an attitude, organization-wide and qualitative; tolerance is a measurable threshold that triggers escalation.

Owner against action owner. The owner manages the whole risk; the action owner owns one agreed action.

Management products

ProductPurpose
PID“To describe how risk will be managed on the project. This includes the specific procedures, techniques, standards, and responsibilities to be applied.”
Project log“A record of identified risks related to the project, including their status and history. It is used to capture and maintain information on all the identified threats and opportunities relating to the project.”
Trap

A tailored procedure, techniques, standards or responsibilities are the approach; the register records risks, their status and history.

Guidance

Risk planning — categories. “The use of risk categories helps projects to identify and prioritize risks. Techniques such as (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental) can be used to analyse the internal and external context for risks and help to identify different types of risk that may affect the project.”

Risk analysis — the . “A useful way of summarizing the set of risks and their estimations is to plot them onto a risk matrix… This represents a situation at a specific point in time (such as a snapshot of the risk environment)… The risks above and to the right of the dashed risk tolerance line represent those that the business will not tolerate, except under special circumstances.”

For risk management to be effective, “risks that might prevent the project from achieving its objectives need to be identified, captured, and described; each risk needs to be assessed and prioritized”.

Risk control — ownership. “The is responsible for the management, monitoring, and control of all aspects of a particular risk assigned to them, including the implementation of the selected responses… The owns an action to address a risk.”

Risk culture and decision bias

“ is natural and largely positive, allowing the brain to efficiently make rapid decisions every day. However, sometimes decision bias can result in less effective decision-making. There are many types of bias, for example:”

BiasOfficial description
“A mindset that drives people to discount disadvantageous risk, on the assumption that things are likely to be successful for them.”
“A mindset that values the avoidance of loss rather than making a gain.”
“A mindset that makes people value social cohesion in a group more than expressing an alternative point of view or reaching the right decision.”
“A mindset where situations that are closer in time are seen as riskier and more important than those in the future.”

Recommended risk response types

For threatsFor opportunities
— “making an uncertain situation certain by removing the risk… by removing the cause of a threat” — making the opportunity certain, “by implementing a factor that leads to an opportunity”
(mitigate) — lower the probability, the impact, or both — increase the probability, the impact, or both
— pass the financial impact to a third party, for example insuranceNo opportunity entry
— both parties share gain and pain — as for threats
— take no action, monitor — take no action to capture it
— actions held ready to be invoked if the risk occurs—
Trap

Transfer is a threat response — the opportunity column has no entry for it. And the opportunity twin of accept is reject, not accept.

Use of data in risk management

Historical data from previous projects informs which risks to expect and how likely they are; live project data shows whether responses are working. Stored past performance can be used to predict future performance, and automation increasingly removes the manual effort of collating it.

Data does not replace judgement — it is what keeps decision bias in check.

The technique: the risk management procedure

StepWhat happens
IdentifyDefine context and objectives“Involves obtaining information about the project to ensure that there is a common understanding of the specific objectives that are at risk and to formulate an appropriate . The following will have an influence on the project’s risk management approach: the business’ own environment (legislative or governance requirements); business policies, standards, processes and procedures.”
IdentifyIdentify the risksFind and describe risks in terms, and record them in the risk register.
AssessPrioritize risksLook at “the probability that the risk will occur (often estimated by considering its likelihood or frequency); the impact of each risk in terms of the project objectives (for example, if the objectives are measured in time and cost, the impact should also be measured in units of time and cost); the impact of the risk on the , , and ”.
AssessThe combined risk profileAssess overall exposure across the whole set of risks, not just individually.
Plan“Involves identifying and evaluating the appropriate risk response to remove or reduce threats, and to maximize opportunities.”
Implement“Planned risk responses need to be actioned, their effectiveness reviewed, and corrective action taken where responses do not match expectations. It is critical to ensure that the responsibilities for the risk owner and risk action owner are identified and agreed for each risk.”
Communicate“Ensures that information related to the threats and opportunities faced by the project is communicated both within the project ecosystem and externally to stakeholders from the .”

The part of the work that deals with what might happen, good or bad.

Part 4.6 is issues, and the line between the two is one of the cheapest marks in the paper. A risk is uncertain and has not happened, and lives in the risk register. An issue is unplanned, has happened, and lives in the issue register. The next sheet also has its own five-step technique, and the two techniques are worth learning as a pair rather than one after the other.

Sheet 10 · Part 4, section 4.6

Issues

The one thing

One question decides half of it: has it happened yet?

Uncertain and not yet happened is a risk. Unplanned and already happened is an issue, and the word unplanned is the giveaway. After that it is four pairs that look alike: a problem is already hurting and a concern still has to be assessed; a request for change asks for an alteration and an off-specification reports a shortfall. And the list everyone gets wrong: there are five types of issue, not three.

Purpose

Purpose

“To collect and assess issues and control changes to the project’s baseline.”

Key concepts

TermDefinition
“An unplanned event that has occurred and requires management action.” “Issues may be raised at any time during the project by any team member or stakeholder.”
“The current approved versions of the management products and specialist products that are subject to change control.”
“A modification to any of the approved products that constitute the project baseline.”
The procedure ensuring changes to baselines are captured, assessed, and approved or rejected in a controlled way.
“An issue with an immediate and negative impact.”
“An issue whose timeliness and impact need to be assessed.”
“A proposal for a change to a baseline.”
“A product that will not meet its quality specifications.” It “represents a discrepancy between the approved project baseline and the delivered products, and this discrepancy must be addressed through the change control procedure”.
Risk against issue

The five types of issue

The assessing step asks the question in exactly these terms: a problem or concern, an event external to the project, a business opportunity, a request for change, or an off-specification.

Material in circulation is wrong

A great deal of the material in circulation teaches three types of issue. The technique lists five:

1 a problem or concern · 2 an event external to the project · 3 a business opportunity · 4 a request for change · 5 an off-specification.

In this way, changes can be made without always having to escalate decisions to the project board for approval.”

. “The project manager should ensure that delegated authority is accompanied by an appropriate change budget from which approved changes can be delivered. The change budget is usually an amount of money earmarked specifically to fund changes. However, it can also be defined as a set of authorized constraints within which trade-offs can be made.”

Authority without a budget is not really authority — it is by applying the change budget that approved changes get funded, and therefore implemented.

Sheet 11 · Part 4, section 4.7

Progress

The one thing

You escalate on a forecast, not on a fact.

An exception is a predicted breach: you raise the report when you can see the limits going, not once they have gone. Everything else hangs off that. Each of the four levels has a box and asks the level above when the box is about to be too small; six reports carry the news and each is either time-driven or event-driven; and step 3’s four options belong to the board, never to the project manager. The sheet ends with all seven practice purposes side by side, which is the one list whose members live on seven different sheets.

Purpose

Purpose — three parts

“To: establish mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements against those planned; provide a forecast for the project’s objectives and continued viability; control any deviations causing an exception.”

The fuller statement

“A key component of project management is controlling the project’s progress, which ensures that the project remains viable against its approved business case. Progress control involves measuring actual progress against the performance targets of benefits, time, cost, quality, scope, sustainability, and risk. This information is used to make decisions such as whether to approve a stage or work package, whether to escalate deviations, or whether to prematurely close the project, and to take actions as required. Progress can be monitored at work package, stage, and project level.”

Key concepts

TermDefinition
The permissible deviation from a plan before escalation. Set on all seven “for the respective level (project, stage, team)” — the team’s limits being the tolerances agreed for its .
“A situation where it can be forecast that there will be a deviation beyond the tolerance levels agreed between the and the (or between the project board and ).”
“A prediction made by studying historical data and past patterns.”
“A management control that occurs when a specific event occurs. For example, this could be the end of a stage, the completion of the , or the creation of an . It could also include organizational events that may affect the project, such as the end of the financial year.”
A control that occurs at regular intervals — the (frequency set in the ) and the (frequency set by the project board).
Trap

An exception is a forecast breach, not an actual one. You escalate when you predict you will go outside tolerance — not when you already have.

Management products

ProductPurpose
Team manager → Project manager · Time-driven“To report to the project manager the status of the work package description at a frequency defined in the work package description.”
Project manager → Project board · Time-driven“To provide the project board (and possibly other stakeholders) with a summary of the stage status at intervals defined by them.”
Project manager → Project board · Event-driven“To give a summary of progress to date, the overall project situation, and sufficient information to ask for a project board decision on what to do next with the project.” Produced at the end of each stage.
Project manager → Project board · Event-driven“To review how the project performed against the version of the used to authorize it.”
Project manager → Project board · Event-drivenRaised “when a project or stage exceeds (or is anticipated to exceed) an agreed tolerance” — describes the exception, its cause, options and a recommendation.
Project manager → Project board or the business · Event-drivenCaptures lessons worth passing on to this project’s later stages and to other projects.
Project logThe project manager’s informal record of actions, events and minor issues.
Project logLessons identified during the project, and drawn from earlier ones.
PID“How data and information will be created, used, and managed across the project ecosystem and through the project lifecycle and afterwards.”

Guidance

Tolerances and the escalation chain. “The , outside the project team, sets the overall requirements and tolerance levels for the project.”

“The has overall control at a project level… If any forecasts indicate that the project is likely to exceed the agreed project tolerances, then the deviation should be referred to the business layer by the project board. This is to decide the corrective action.”

“The has day-to-day control of a stage within the tolerance limits established by the project board.”

“The has control for a work package, but only within the work package tolerances agreed with the project manager.”

Reviewing and reporting. “As part of the ‘’ process, the project manager will regularly review progress through checkpoint reports and will maintain the .” A is “information to facilitate the future of the project or other projects and actively promote learning from experience”.

Forecasting. Forecasting is what makes possible: you escalate on the basis of where the stage is heading, not where it has got to. Every progress review therefore asks two questions — what has actually been achieved against plan, and what that implies for the final cost and date, scope and benefits. “Progress reviews are not confined to looking backwards.”

Escalating. “When a project or stage exceeds (or is anticipated to exceed) an agreed tolerance, a project manager will raise an exception report to the project board.” And upward from there: “if the forecast is for project tolerances to be exceeded, the project board no longer has the authority to direct the project and must refer the matter to the business layer for a decision. The project board may request the project manager to produce an for the project.”

Use of data and systems. “Data and technology help manage projects more accurately by supporting progress tracking and decision-making.” “After having secured and stored the data through systems, past performance can be used to predict future performance. To ensure clarity, this information can then be presented in the stakeholders’ preferred format and style.”

“Automation, for example the use of artificial intelligence, is removing the need for a manual approach, enabling project professionals to focus on far more value-added tasks rather than administration.”

Data and systems do not set the tolerances — the do.

The technique: exception management

StepWhat happens
Step 1The project manager assesses it“If the issue can be resolved by the project manager within the stage tolerances, the resolution will not require an exception report to be created.” It is simply reported in the next highlight report.
Step 2The project manager raises itIf a stage tolerance is forecast to be breached, the project manager raises an exception report to the project board, setting out the cause, the options and a recommendation.
Step 3The board decides“The project board or have several options that they could take.” They may accept or reject the recommendation; they “may reallocate the overall project tolerances to resolve the breach of the stage tolerance”; they may request an exception plan; or they may escalate “to the business layer for advice and direction, if the exception will take the project outside one or more of its project level tolerances”.

Where do exceptions arise? “Issues are often encountered in the delivering level of the project that will take the stage outside one of the stage tolerances. It may also occur at the managing and directing levels for those issues that are not driven from delivery problems.”

Trap

Step 3’s options belong to the project board or project executive, never the project manager.

And step 1 is an anti-escalation rule: if it can be fixed inside stage tolerance, there is no exception report at all.

The seven purposes, side by side

PracticePurpose
To establish mechanisms to judge whether the project is (and remains) desirable, viable, and achievable as a means to support decision-making in its continued investment.
To define and establish the project’s structure of accountability and responsibilities (the “who”).
To facilitate communication and control by defining the products to be delivered and the means to deliver them, to satisfy the project business case.
To document the user’s requirements of the project products and to establish the means by which they will be met.
To identify, assess, and control uncertainties that would affect the project’s objectives and, as a result, improve the ability of the project to succeed.
To collect and assess issues and control changes to the project’s baseline.
To establish mechanisms to monitor and compare actual achievements against those planned; provide a forecast for the project’s objectives and continued viability; and control any deviations causing an exception.

Sheet 12 · Part 5

The seven processes

The one thing

Same method, other axis: the practices are what, the processes are when.

Each process is examined on three separate things — its purpose, its objectives, its context — and answering one with another is how the marks go. Then eight beliefs that sound right and are not, and almost all of them are about which process owns a thing: highlight reporting is CS and not the boundary, agreeing the work is MP and not CS, reviewing the business case is CS too, assessing realized benefits is CP, and closing a project is not a stage at all.

Purpose, objectives and context

Each process is described three ways, and they are three different questions.

ColumnWhat it answers
PurposeWhy the process exists, in one sentence.
ObjectivesThe specific things it must achieve — usually a list beginning “to ensure that…”.
ContextWhen it runs, what triggers it, who leads it, and how it relates to the others.

The shape of the lifecycle

ProcessWho leads, and when
SU or — pre-project, before the decision to start.
DP — throughout, from the end of SU to closure.
IP — the initiation stage, once.
CS — every delivery stage, repeatedly.
MP — every delivery stage, alongside CS.
SB — near the end of each stage except the last; also to produce an .

5.1 · Starting up a project SU

Purpose

“To ensure that the prerequisites for ‘initiating a project’ are established by answering the question, ‘Do we have a viable and worthwhile project?’ The decision to start the project must be explicit, as the activities within the process of starting up a project happen before this decision.”

Objectives

  • there is a business justification for initiating the project, documented in an ;
  • the necessary authorities exist for initiating the project;
  • “sufficient information is available to define and confirm the scope of the project (in the form of a )”;
  • “alternative approaches have been evaluated and the chosen project approach agreed”;
  • individuals are appointed to the roles needed for initiation and for the project;
  • the work required for initiation is planned, in an initiation ;
  • time is not wasted initiating a project based on unsound assumptions.

Context

“In PRINCE2 Project Management, the trigger for the project is referred to as the . This is provided by the responsible authority from the business that is commissioning the project.” The mandate “activates the process of starting up a project” and is “used as an input to develop the initial business justification for the project documented in the outline business case”.

SU is pre-project — it happens before there is authority to proceed. It ends with a request to the to initiate the project. The is created here and refined in IP.

The half of the purpose people forget

“The purpose of the process of starting up a project is as much about preventing poorly conceived ideas from ever being initiated as it is about progressing viable projects for approval. As such, ‘starting up a project’ is a lighter process compared to the more detailed and thorough process of initiating a project. The aim is to do the minimum necessary to decide whether it is worthwhile to even initiate the project.”

5.2 · Directing a project DP

Purpose

“To enable the project board to be accountable for the project’s success by making key decisions and exercising overall control while delegating day-to-day management of the project to the project manager.”

Objectives

  • “there is authority to initiate the project”;
  • “there is authority to deliver the project product”;
  • “there is authority to close the project”;
  • “plans for realizing the post-project are managed and reviewed”;
  • management direction and control are provided throughout, and the project remains viable;
  • the has an interface to the project.

Context

DP runs from the end of SU to the end of the project. The board , so it is not involved day to day, and not absent either: “one of the functions of the project board is to provide informal advice and guidance as well as formal direction to the project manager. This is a two-way process, with the project board updating the project manager on matters external to the project and the project manager seeking advice whenever necessary during the course of the project.”

The board’s authority has a ceiling: “if the forecast is for project tolerances to be exceeded, the project board no longer has the authority to direct the project and must refer the matter to the business layer for a decision.”

Four to have cold

Three authorities — initiate, deliver, close — plus post-project benefits.

5.3 · Initiating a project IP

Purpose

“To establish solid foundations for the project, enabling the business to understand the work that needs to be done to deliver the project product before committing to any significant expenditure or resources.”

Objectives

  • the reasons for doing the project, the benefits expected and the associated risks;
  • the of what is to be done and the products to be delivered;
  • “how and when the products will be delivered and at what cost”;
  • who is to be involved in project decision-making;
  • “how the quality required will be achieved”;
  • “how baselines will be established and controlled”;
  • how risks, issues and changes will be identified, assessed and controlled;
  • “how progress will be monitored and controlled”;
  • who needs information, in what format and at what time;
  • how the PRINCE2 method will be .

Context

Every objective in this process begins with the stem “to ensure there is a common understanding of”.

IP happens once, in the initiation stage, after the board authorizes initiation. It produces the , including the — which is “created during the process of initiating the project and baselined upon its approval by the project board”. The project product description is refined here. IP ends with a request to deliver the project.

Trap

Confusing IP’s purpose with SU’s. SU asks whether to bother, and does the minimum; IP asks what is being committed to, and is thorough.

5.4 · Controlling a stage CS

Purpose

“To assign work, monitor such work, handle issues, report progress to the project board, and take corrective actions to ensure that the stage remains within the tolerances set by the project board.”

Objectives

  • “attention is focused on delivery of the stage’s products”;
  • “any movement away from the products and delivery method that was agreed at the start of the stage is monitored to avoid uncontrolled change”;
  • “the agreed products for the stage meet the agreed quality expectations and are accepted”;
  • “risks and issues are controlled”;
  • “the is kept under review”;
  • the project management team is focused on delivery within the agreed tolerances.

Context

“Normally the process of ‘controlling a stage’ is used first after the project board authorizes the project, but it can be used during the initiation stage, especially for large or complex projects.”

“If the project manager is fulfilling the role, should still be used to define and control the work of the individual team members.”

CS and SB are not merged — SB’s activities occur towards the end of each stage, with the exception of the final stage.

Highlight reporting is a CS activity: “reporting highlights to the project board at an agreed frequency” is carried out in controlling a stage, not at the stage boundary.

5.5 · Managing product delivery MP

Purpose

“To control the link between the project manager and the team manager. This is achieved by agreeing on the requirements for acceptance, execution, reporting, and delivery of specialist products. The role of the team manager is to coordinate an area of work that will deliver one or more of the specialist products that form the project product.”

Objectives

  • work on the products allocated to the team is authorized and agreed;
  • the team manager, team members and suppliers are clear what is to be produced, and the expected effort, cost and timescales;
  • the planned products are delivered to expectations and within tolerance;
  • accurate progress information is provided to the project manager at an agreed frequency.

Context

MP runs alongside CS through every delivery stage. The team manager receives a from the project manager, may produce an optional , and reports back through at the frequency defined in the work package description. “Team managers can be internal or external to the organization running the project.”

Trap

The team manager agrees the work in MP; CS is the project manager’s side of the conversation — assigning, monitoring, reporting, correcting.

5.6 · Managing a stage boundary SB

Purpose

“To enable the project manager to provide the project board with sufficient information to be able to: review the success of the current stage; approve the next stage plan; review the updated project plan; confirm continued business justification and acceptability of the risks.”

Objectives

  • “Assure the project board that all products in the current stage plan have been completed and approved.”
  • “Prepare a or for the next stage.”
  • “Review and, if necessary, update the , in particular the business case, project plan, user’s quality expectations, management approaches, project management team structure, and role descriptions.”
  • Provide the information the board needs to assess continuing viability, including aggregated .
  • Record any information or lessons useful to later stages or other projects.
  • Request authorization to start the next stage.

Context

For exceptions: “the objectives… are similar to those listed above but include preparing an exception plan and seeking approval to replace the project or current stage plan with the exception plan.”

“The process of managing a stage boundary is based on dividing the project into stages.” That is its foundation — not exceptions.

“The process of managing a stage boundary provides a means by which an exception procedure can be implemented.” A request for an exception plan is a trigger for SB.

Its activities occur “towards the end of each stage… with the exception of the final stage”.

Purpose against objective

The purpose says the board can approve the next stage plan. The objective says the project manager will prepare a stage plan or exception plan.

Purpose is what the board can do with the information. Objective is what the project manager produces.

5.7 · Closing a project CP

Purpose

“To provide a fixed point at which acceptance of the project product is confirmed. It also provides a point to recognize that the objectives or the approved changes to the objectives, as established in the project initiation documentation, have been achieved. Where there is a cause for a premature closure, this process ensures the project is closed in an orderly way.”

Objectives

  • “Check user acceptance of the project product.”
  • “Ensure that the business can support the products when the project is closed.”
  • “Assess any benefits that have already been realized” and update the with post-project benefit reviews.
  • Review the performance of the project against its baselines.
  • Ensure provision has been made to address all open issues and risks, with follow-on action recommendations.
  • “Ensure the project is closed in an orderly way and not simply abandoned (in the case of a premature close).”

Context

Why the process exists at all: “One of the defining features of a project is that it is finite; it has a start and an end. If the project loses this distinction, it loses some of its advantages over purely operational management approaches.”

“A clear end to a project is always more successful than a slow drift into use, as it is a recognition by all concerned that project costs should no longer be incurred.”

Premature closure is the board’s call: “It is also possible that the project board may wish to trigger a premature closure of the project under some circumstances; for example, if the business case is no longer valid. If the project is being brought to a premature closure, this process will still need to be executed” — though it “may have to be tailored to the project situation”.

CP is carried out as the final part of the last management stage. It is not a stage of its own — which is why SB is not performed at the end of the final stage. Preparing for premature closure is a CP activity, not an SB one.

At acceptance, “ownership or responsibility for the product [transfers] from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user”. At transition, “there are three key aspects the project board needs to consider: products, people, and learning”.

Believed against actually

BelievedActually
Closing a project is a separate final stageIt is the final part of the last stage. SB is skipped at the end of the final stage precisely because CP takes its place.
Controlling a stage only starts after authorization“Normally”, yes — but it can be used during the initiation stage on large or complex projects.
The team manager agrees the work in controlling a stageIn managing product delivery.
The business case is only reviewed at stage boundaries“The business case is kept under review” is an explicit objective of controlling a stage too.
Highlight reporting happens at the stage boundaryIt happens in controlling a stage, at a frequency the board sets. The is the boundary product.
Directing a project only happens at decision pointsIt runs throughout, and includes informal, two-way advice and guidance.
Managing a stage boundary exists to handle exceptionsIt is based on dividing the project into stages; handling exceptions is a capability it provides.
Assessing realized benefits happens at a stage boundaryIt is an objective of closing a project.

Answer these out loud before you look anything up
  1. Name the seven processes in order with their abbreviations, and say who leads each and when it runs.
  2. Give the purpose of starting up a project, then give the half of it that is about stopping things rather than starting them.
  3. What triggers starting up a project, who provides that trigger, and what is it used to develop?
  4. Distinguish the purpose of SU from the purpose of IP. Which is deliberately light, and which is deliberately thorough?
  5. Name the three authorities that are objectives of directing a project, and the fourth thing the board is accountable for.
  6. Which process is highlight reporting carried out in, at whose frequency, and which report is the boundary product instead?
  7. Which process does the team manager agree what is to be produced in, and what is the project manager doing in the other one?
  8. What is managing a stage boundary based on, and what is the thing it merely provides a means for? When are its activities not performed?
  9. Is closing a project a stage? Say what it is instead, and what follows from that about the end of the final stage.
  10. Two objectives are commonly put on the wrong process: reviewing the business case, and assessing realized benefits. Say which process each one actually belongs to.

Sheet 13 · Part 6

Reference tables

The one thing

Nothing new — everything sorted the other way.

Sheets 04 to 12 sort the method by practice. This one sorts it by document, by report, by technique and by role, which is how a question tends to arrive: it hands you a document and asks which folder it lives in, or a report and asks who sends it to whom. Two folders carry almost everything — the PID is how the project will be run, the project log is what has happened — and thirteen products sit in neither.

Inside the PID — “how we will manage this project”

ProductOne-line purpose
Establish the target organizational state and how the business shifts from the current state through any interim states.
The means and frequency of communication and feedback — a controlled, bidirectional flow of information.
The benefits management actions and benefits reviews that confirm outcomes are achieved and benefits realized.
How sustainability objectives are managed, measured and reported.
How commercial and supplier relationships are managed.
The quality techniques and standards to be applied, and the roles and responsibilities for achieving the required quality specifications and acceptance criteria.
How risk will be managed — the specific procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities.
How issues will be captured and reported, and how changes to the project baseline will be assessed and controlled.
How data and information will be created, used and managed across the project ecosystem and afterwards.
High-level plan of the major products and when, how and at what cost they will be delivered.
The business justification — estimated costs against expected benefits, offset by associated risks.
Who is involved, their relationships, and how they will work together.
The roles in the project management team and their specific responsibilities, including accountability for sustainability targets.
What the user expects of the project product — reviewed and updated at stage boundaries.
& decisionsReporting frequencies, tolerances, and how PRINCE2 has been tailored for this project.

Quality planning (its activities include gathering user inputs and describing the quality management approach) → Controlling quality → Accepting products
— risk management procedure
Identify (define context and objectives; identify the risks) → Assess (prioritize risks; combined risk profile) → Plan → Implement → Communicate
— issue management
Capturing issues → Assessing issues → Recommending → Deciding on changes → Implementing changes
— exception management
Step 1 resolve within tolerance if possible → Step 2 raise an exception report → Step 3 the board or executive decides

Sheet 15 · Waterfall, agile and everything around them

Ways of working

The one thing

decides everything up front. decides the next bit and stays ready to be wrong.

Your job changes shape between the two — one large document versus a continuous conversation. Neither is correct in general; they suit different amounts of uncertainty.

Around the method 2

SDLCprocess

The whole journey a piece of software goes through, from someone first having the idea to the day it gets switched off. Software Development Life Cycle. It's the container; and are two different ways of moving through it.

In the proper languageSoftware Development Life Cycle. The sequence of phases — typically initiation, , design, build, test, deploy, operate, retire — within which a delivery methodology operates.

DevOpsprocess

A way of organising so that the people who build software and the people who run it are one team rather than two who blame each other. In practice it mostly means heavy automation — code gets built, tested and released by machines rather than by a person doing it by hand at midnight.

In the proper languagePractice development and operations through shared ownership, automation and continuous integration and delivery pipelines, reducing lead time and deployment risk.

The shapes 3

Waterfallprocess

Doing the strictly one after another: work everything out, write it all down, build it all, test it all, release it. Changing your mind late is expensive, because everything downstream was built on the earlier decisions.

In the proper languageSequential delivery with defined phase gates and a fully specified established before build; PRINCE2 is not a synonym for waterfall, being a management method that sits above any delivery shape.

Agileprocess

Building in small pieces, showing each piece to people quickly, and expecting to change your mind as you learn. Suits situations where nobody yet knows exactly what's needed.

In the proper languageIterative and incremental delivery approach prioritising working software, customer collaboration and responsiveness to change over comprehensive up-front . An umbrella term rather than a single method.

Hybrid deliveryprocess

Running part of a project the waterfall way and part of it the agile way. Very common in big organisations, where the money and the deadlines are agreed up front like waterfall but the building happens in sprints.

In the proper languageDelivery approach combining sequential and iterative elements, typically applying stage-gated governance and fixed funding at programme level with agile execution at team level.

Scrum 4

Scrumprocess

The most common specific way of doing . Work happens in fixed short blocks with a defined set of meetings and three defined roles.

In the proper language framework structuring delivery into fixed-length with prescribed roles (, , Developers), events and .

Sprintprocess

A fixed block of time, usually two weeks, in which a team commits to finishing an agreed amount of work. Once it starts, nothing new gets added.

In the proper languageTime-boxed iteration of fixed duration producing a potentially releasable increment. Sprint is protected from change once committed.

Scrum Masterrole

The person responsible for the process running properly and for clearing obstacles out of the team's way. Not a manager of people.

In the proper language role accountable for the framework being understood and enacted, facilitating events, coaching the team and removing impediments.

Ceremoniesprocess

The fixed set of meetings in : planning at the start, a short daily catch-up, a review to show what got built, and a retrospective to discuss how the team is working.

In the proper languageThe prescribed events — planning, daily scrum, sprint review and sprint retrospective — each time-boxed with a defined purpose.

Kanban 1

Kanbanprocess

A way of working with no at all — work just flows through columns on a board continuously. Its key rule is limiting how many things can be in progress at once, which stops everything being started and nothing being finished.

In the proper languageFlow-based method using a visual board, explicit work-in-progress limits and continuous delivery rather than fixed iterations. Well suited to support and business-as-usual work with unpredictable arrival rates.

  4. Who owns the backlog?

Sheet 16 · The words that aren't about process

Technical literacy

The one thing

You don't need to build any of this. You need enough of it to know what you're asking for.

Your notes had a lot of technical vocabulary with nowhere obvious to sit, so it lives here. The bar is being able to hold a conversation with a developer without nodding along blankly.

Systems and data 4

APIdefinition

The way two pieces of software talk to each other. Application Programming Interface. Think of it as a hatch in the side of a system with a fixed set of things you're allowed to ask for — you don't get to reach inside and rummage, you ask through the hatch in the agreed format.

In the proper languageApplication Programming Interface. A defined contract exposing a set of operations, request and response formats, and authentication , enabling systems to exchange data without knowledge of internal implementation.

Integrationdefinition

Connecting two systems so that information moves between them automatically instead of somebody re-typing it.

In the proper languageThe connection of discrete systems to exchange data or invoke functions, implemented via , message queues, file transfer or middleware.

SQLdefinition

The language used to ask questions of a database. Structured Query Language. A doesn't usually need to write much, but being able to check a number yourself rather than waiting three days for someone else to check it is a genuine advantage.

In the proper languageStructured Query Language. Declarative language for querying and manipulating relational . For analysts, principally used for data profiling, and reconciliation.

ERPdefinition

One large system that runs most of a company's core operations — finance, stock, purchasing, HR — in one place instead of separate systems that don't talk. Enterprise Resource Planning. and are examples.

In the proper languageEnterprise Resource Planning. suite covering core business functions on a shared , typically requiring significant configuration and process alignment during implementation.

Sheet 18 · Not in your notes

The gaps

Why this sheet exists

CVs list what is listable.

Tools, certificates and job titles fit neatly on a CV. The concepts holding a field together mostly do not, so your sheets have holes in predictable places. Every term below is defined in the glossary, not on the sheets themselves — this is the chase-up list, grouped by topic.

Stakeholders and responsibility 2
  • — A way of ranking stakeholders on two questions: how much can they affect this, and how much do they care? The ones high on both get your attention; the ones low on both get an email.
  • — A grid saying, for each task, who does it, who signs it off, who gets consulted and who just needs telling. Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed.
Ready, and done 2
  • — A checklist a piece of work has to pass before a team will agree to start it. Stops half-formed requests being pulled into a .
  • — A checklist a piece of work has to pass before anyone is allowed to call it finished. Different from : acceptance criteria are specific to one , the definition of done applies to every story.
Agile in practice 6
  • — The ordered list of everything that hasn't been built yet. Constantly reordered and refined; never finished.
  • — The ongoing job of breaking big items down, adding detail and re-ordering, so that the next things to be picked up are ready to go.
  • — The person who decides what gets built next and in what order. If you become a in an team, this is the role you work most closely with — and often the one you eventually move into.
  • — A framework for running across many teams at once in a big organisation. Scaled Agile Framework. Turns up constantly on job adverts for large employers.
  • — A cap on how many jobs can be underway at the same time. Counter-intuitive but it makes things finish faster, because starting a fifth job doesn't make the first four go quicker.
  • — The automated pipeline underneath . Every time someone changes the code it's automatically combined with everyone else's, tested, and pushed towards release.
General literacy 10
  • — A map of what information the system holds and how the different pieces relate to each other — a customer has many orders, each order has many items.
  • — The diagram of a . Entity Relationship Diagram. Boxes for the kinds of thing stored, lines for how they connect.
  • — The four things you can do to any record: Create, Read, Update, Delete. Comes up constantly when what a user is allowed to do.
  • — An organised store of information that software reads from and writes to. Usually arranged as tables with rows and columns, like a very strict spreadsheet.
  • — A short written sketch of a typical user — what they're trying to do, what gets in their way. Used so that discussions are about a specific person rather than a vague “the user”.
  • — A deliberately rough sketch of a screen layout, showing where things go without any styling. Rough on purpose, so people comment on the structure rather than the colours.
  • — Horizontal bands across a process diagram, one per person or team. They show who does what — and every point where work crosses from one band to another is a handover, which is where things usually go wrong.
  • — The actual form or ticket raised when someone wants something added or altered after was agreed.
  • — Running software on someone else's computers, rented by the hour, instead of on machines your company owns and keeps in a cupboard.
  • — Business as usual. The ordinary day-to-day running of things, as opposed to a project that changes them.
Ignore these — padding, not concepts 4
  • — Situation, Task, Action, Result. A structure for answering interview questions about your experience. It is not a technique, despite appearing on a CV as though it were.
  • — A very broad phrase for an organisation changing how it works by using technology differently. It describes a programme of activity rather than any particular technique, so there is not much underneath it to learn.
  • — Making an existing process work better — faster, cheaper, fewer mistakes. Again this names an activity rather than a specific method; the methods are things like Lean and .
  • — Siemens engineering design software, used for drawing physical products in 3D. Nothing to do with — it tells you which industry that person worked in.

Glossary

A business opportunity (issue type)concept

Acceptance criteriadefinition

Accepting products (quality technique)technique

Ownership changes hands, once it has been looked at against what was asked for.

Agileprocess

Building in small pieces, showing each piece to people quickly, and expecting to change your mind as you learn. Suits situations where nobody yet knows exactly what's needed.

An event external to the project (issue type)concept

Something outside the job that lands on it anyway.

Analysisdefinition

Breaking something complicated into parts you can look at one at a time, then working out what those parts mean together. The opposite of taking a situation at face value.

Anticipating requirements changesconcept

However carefully you asked, it will change.

APIdefinition

The way two pieces of software talk to each other. Application Programming Interface. Think of it as a hatch in the side of a system with a fixed set of things you're allowed to ask for — you don't get to reach inside and rummage, you ask through the hatch in the agreed format.

In the proper languageApplication Programming Interface. A defined contract exposing a set of operations, request and response formats, and authentication , enabling systems to exchange data without knowledge of internal implementation.

Artefactdefinition

Just a formal word for a thing you produce — a document, a diagram, a spreadsheet. When someone says “ artefacts” they mean “the documents the analyst made”.

As-isdefinition

How the process really works today. Not how the official document says it works — those two are almost never the same, and the difference is usually the most interesting thing you'll find.

Work out how likely and how bad each one is.

Add them all up and look at the total.

In the proper languageAssess overall across the whole set of risks, not just individually.

What kind is it, does it matter, how much.

Fix it yourself and no alarm goes off.

Assumption

Something everyone is treating as true without having actually checked. Usually the most dangerous line on the log.

The agreed version of everything, frozen. It can still change, but only by asking and being told yes.

Business as usual. The ordinary day-to-day running of things, as opposed to a project that changes them.

Going back after the change is live to check whether the promised in the actually happened. Almost nobody does it, which is why so many projects can claim success.

How far short the promised improvement may fall before you have to go and tell someone.

A standard set of shapes for drawing business processes, so that everyone reads the same diagram the same way. Stands for Business and Notation.

Business analysisdefinition

Working out what a business actually needs, then describing it clearly enough that someone else can build it. You sit between the people who have a problem and the people who can fix it, and your job is to make sure nothing gets lost in between.

Business interestconcept

The side paying for it, and the side that has to keep getting its money’s worth.

The formal yes before something is allowed to go live. Someone with authority reviews what is being released, what could go wrong, and how you would undo it if it does. Even finished, fully tested work waits for this.

Money set aside to pay for approved changes.

Getting people to actually take up the new thing. It has nothing to do with editing documents.

The written plan for moving people onto the new way of working.

In the proper language

A written proposal to change something that had already been agreed. Writing it down is the point: it forces someone with authority to say yes or no, rather than the change just happening.

Keep testing the argument as the facts change, right through to the last stage.

Checkpoint reportdocument

How one team’s parcel of work is going.

Closing a project (CP)process

A definite end, rather than a slow fade into everyday use.

Carried out as the final part of the last management stage. Premature closure is the ’s call, “for example, if the business case is no longer valid”, and the process “will still need to be executed”.

You find what is missing and teach the people you have, because swapping them out is usually not on offer.

Commercial management approachapproach

How outside firms and money are handled: who is paid for what, on what terms.

Concerndefinition

The people who actually build the thing — developers, testers, sometimes operations staff.

DevOpsprocess

A way of organising so that the people who build software and the people who run it are one team rather than two who blame each other. In practice it mostly means heavy automation — code gets built, tested and released by machines rather than by a person doing it by hand at midnight.

Digital transformationdefinition

The people who decide whether it carries on, inside limits set above them.

Tell the deciders; and if it is bigger than them, they have to tell the people above.

People are given room to move and left alone inside it. They go back up only when that room is about to run out.

Features and benefits of PRINCE2concept

It fits any kind of work, it gives everyone the same words, and it keeps the managing separate from the making.

In the proper language

Generic and flexible
Its “strength is its flexibility and the fact that it is not specific to a particular industry, type of project, commercial model, project lifecycle, delivery method, product development, or engineering practice”.
A common vocabulary
It “provides a common vocabulary for all participants, which encourages consistency and the ability to reuse project assets, facilitate staff mobility, and reduce the impact of personnel changes or handovers”.
Management separated from specialist work
It tells you how to manage a project, not how to build the thing.
Four structural features
, , and — following from the principles.

The trapA common vocabulary is not a fixed one: “in general, it may be necessary to tailor the PRINCE2 Project Management terminology to what is common in the company or in the industry in which the project is taking place”.

Backwards.

Something the system has to do. “The user can reset their password by email.”

Future statedefinition

The difference between how it works now and how it should work, plus what it would take to close that difference. This is usually the thing you actually hand over.

Gateways

Government Digital Service. The UK government body that sets the rules for how public-sector digital services must be built — the Service Standard and the Service Manual. If you ever work on a government project, this governs everything you do.

Governancenot in your notesprocess

Groupthinkconcept

Keeping the peace in the room instead of saying the awkward thing.

Guiding obligationprinciple

A rule you do not opt out of. Every one of them holds on every job, each has already been shown to work, and each gives you something to stand on when you push back.

In the proper language

The principles are guiding obligations. They are universal (they apply to every project), self-validating (they have been proven in practice) and empowering (they give practitioners confidence and the ability to influence).

Highlight reportdocument

Hybridapproach

Some parts of the same job built one way, other parts the other.

The period right after something goes live when the project team stays on hand with extra support, before handing over to the normal helpdesk. Usually a few weeks. It exists because the first fortnight is when everything nobody thought of shows up.

Working out what else a change will touch before you make it — other systems, other teams, reports, processes nobody mentioned. It's how you avoid breaking three things to fix one.

Manage by exceptionprinciple

You are told how far off course you may go, and you go back up only before you exceed it.

In the proper language

“A PRINCE2 Project Management project establishes limits of delegated authority by defining tolerances for performance against its plans.”

It works by “delegating authority from one management level to the next, by setting against the seven aspects of performance (benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability, and risk) for the respective level (project, stage, team)”. Manage by stagesprinciple

A is “the section of a project that the is managing on behalf of the at any one time”. Managing by stages “ensures that the project is properly initiated before work starts on delivery of the project’s outputs”, and it “addresses the need to keep plans within reasonable ”.

Every PRINCE2 project has a minimum of two management stages: an initiation stage, plus at least one delivery stage.

Mermaid / Mermaid AIsoftware

Two related things. Mermaid itself is a way of making diagrams by typing text instead of dragging shapes — you write a few lines describing the steps and it draws the flowchart. Mermaid AI is the paid layer on top: you describe what you want in plain English and it writes those lines for you, then draws it.

You wrote “Mermaid Ai?” with a question mark. I first told you it wasn’t an AI tool — that was wrong. The CV was right.

Non-functional requirementdefinition

How well the system has to do it, rather than what it does. Speed, security, how often it's allowed to be down, whether a blind person can use it. “It must be fast” is not one of these. “Search returns results in under two seconds with five hundred people using it at once” is.

In the proper languageA requirement specifying a quality attribute or constraint rather than a function — performance, availability, security, scalability, accessibility, maintainability, regulatory compliance. Must be stated with measurable thresholds to be testable.

Check it was accepted and can be kept running, and tidy up what is left open.

Ten things everyone has to understand the same way, before real money is spent.

Every objective begins “to ensure there is a common understanding of”:

Seven things to have before you may begin: a reason, permission, scope, an approach, people, a plan, and no wasted time.

Observationtechnique

Watching people do the job rather than asking them about it. Catches all the steps people have stopped noticing they do, which is usually where the problems hide.

In the proper language by direct observation of work as performed, sometimes called job shadowing. Effective at surfacing tacit knowledge and workarounds absent from documented process.

Something built that will not be good enough.

In the proper language“A product that will not meet its .” It “represents a discrepancy between the approved project baseline and the delivered products, and this discrepancy must be addressed through the procedure”.

OOdefinition

Object-oriented. A way of building software where you model things in the real world as self-contained objects with their own data and behaviour. was designed to draw it.

In the proper languageObject-oriented and design. Paradigm structuring systems as collaborating objects encapsulating state and behaviour, with inheritance and polymorphism.

Assuming it will be fine for you, whatever the odds say.

A rulebook for running a piece of work: who decides what, at which points, and on what evidence. It does not say how to build anything — only how to stay in control of the building.

The seven rules a project has to keep to.

How urgently it needs fixing. A business judgement. These two often disagree: a spelling mistake on the homepage is barely broken at all but might need fixing this afternoon.

Something already hurting, right now.

Writing down what is actually wrong before anyone proposes a fix. Sounds obvious, and it is the step skipped most often — people arrive with a already in mind and the problem gets written backwards to justify it.

Everyone who has to give the work time, whatever their job title is elsewhere.
